variable-x.t: Look at houses. Let **X = the number of bedrooms**: 1, 2 or 3. Each house has one value of X.

variable-y.t: Each house also has a price band. Let **Y = Low or High**. Now every house carries **two values at once**.

pair-values.t: Together the two variables give pairs: **(1, Low), (1, High), (2, Low)** and so on. With 3 × 2 choices there are **6 possible pairs**, one per cell of a table.

grid.t: Each cell stands for one combination. The highlighted cell is the pair **(3 bedrooms, High price)**. We want a probability for every cell.

joint-probabilities.t: **P(X = x, Y = y)** is the probability of both happening together. For example **P(X = 3, Y = High) = 0.25**: 25% of all houses. All six cells **add up to 1**.

pattern.t: Small houses are mostly Low priced (**0.25 versus 0.05**); big houses are mostly High (**0.25 versus 0.05**). The numbers are not spread evenly, so the variables are **related**.

ml-features.t: A dataset is a pile of samples from a **joint distribution**: each row holds several variables at once. Models learn how features relate by learning about this **joint behavior**.
